questions.prompt: Explain why the volume of a cone is ⅓πr²h, using pyramids.
questions.prompt_markup: Explain why the volume of a cone is ⅓πr²h, using pyramids.
questions.correct_answer: Pyramids with regular n-gon bases inscribed in the circle have V = ⅓Bh; as n grows, B approaches πr² and the pyramids approach the cone, so V = ⅓πr²h.
questions.required_method: Think of pyramids whose bases are regular polygons with more and more sides.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: pyramid volume ⅓Bh; base polygons approach the circle (B → πr²); the pyramids approach the cone. Alternative: Cavalieri comparison with a pyramid of equal base area and height.

questions.prompt: A cone has base radius r and height h. A square pyramid has base area πr² and the same height h. Use Cavalieri's principle to explain why the cone's volume is ⅓πr²h.
questions.prompt_markup: A cone has base radius r and height h. A square pyramid has base area πr² and the same height h. Use Cavalieri's principle to explain why the cone's volume is ⅓πr²h.
questions.correct_answer: At height y both cross-sections are copies of the bases scaled by (h - y)/h, so both have area πr²((h - y)/h)²; equal areas at every level and equal heights give equal volumes, ⅓πr²h.
questions.required_method: Compare the cross-section areas of the two solids at the same height y.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the scale factor (h - y)/h for both solids; equal cross-section areas; Cavalieri's principle; the pyramid formula ⅓Bh with B = πr².

questions.prompt: In an experiment, three cones full of water exactly fill a cylinder with the same base radius and height. Explain what this shows about the cone formula and why it is evidence, not a proof.
questions.prompt_markup: In an experiment, three cones full of water exactly fill a cylinder with the same base radius and height. Explain what this shows about the cone formula and why it is evidence, not a proof.
questions.correct_answer: One cone holds about ⅓ of πr²h, which supports V = ⅓πr²h; the experiment has measurement error and tests one cone, so it does not prove the formula.
questions.required_method: Relate the cylinder volume πr²h to the three cone fillings, then discuss measurement.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the ⅓ relationship with the cylinder; evidence versus proof.

questions.prompt: A cone with radius r and height h is approximated by n stacked disks of thickness h/n; the disk k steps from the top has radius kr/n. The total disk volume is (πr²h/n³) × (the sum of the squares 1², 2², 3², and so on up to n²), which equals 0.385πr²h for n = 10 and 0.338πr²h for n = 100. Explain how this supports V = ⅓πr²h.
questions.prompt_markup: A cone with radius r and height h is approximated by n stacked disks of thickness h/n; the disk k steps from the top has radius kr/n. The total disk volume is (πr²h/n³) × (the sum of the squares 1², 2², 3², and so on up to n²), which equals 0.385πr²h for n = 10 and 0.338πr²h for n = 100. Explain how this supports V = ⅓πr²h.
questions.correct_answer: As the disks get thinner they fit the cone more closely, and the coefficients approach ⅓, so V = ⅓πr²h.
questions.required_method: Describe what the disks approach and what the coefficients approach.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the disks approximate the cone better as n grows; the trend toward ⅓; conclusion.

questions.prompt: A cone has base radius r and height h. A plane parallel to the base cuts the cone at height y above the base. Explain why the cross-section is a circle of radius r(h - y)/h, and why this fact is what makes the cone's volume ⅓ of the cylinder's rather than ½.
questions.prompt_markup: A cone has base radius r and height h. A plane parallel to the base cuts the cone at height y above the base. Explain why the cross-section is a circle of radius r(h - y)/h, and why this fact is what makes the cone's volume ⅓ of the cylinder's rather than ½.
questions.correct_answer: The small cone above the cut is similar to the whole cone with ratio (h - y)/h, so the radius is r(h - y)/h. The areas shrink like the SQUARE of that ratio, πr²((h - y)/h)², so most of the volume is near the base and the total is ⅓πr²h, less than the ½ a linear shrink would suggest.
questions.required_method: Use similar triangles in a vertical cross-section through the apex; compare how the cross-section areas shrink.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: similar triangles give the radius; area scales by the square of the ratio; link to the ⅓ factor (via Cavalieri or slab sums).
